title: Capriccio espagnol
hook: Spain imagined by a Russian, in fifteen minutes of castanets, fanfares and solo cadenzas.

painting.title: The Dance on the Banks of the Manzanares
painting.pairingNote: Two majos and two majas dance seguidillas to guitars by the river in Madrid, in one of Goya’s first designs for royal tapestries; the Spanish street dances that Rimsky-Korsakov’s themes come from.

facts: Rimsky-Korsakov wrote the Capriccio in the summer of 1887, at a rented villa on a lake near Luga, south of St Petersburg. He was spending that summer orchestrating his late friend Borodin’s opera *Prince Igor*, and broke off to write it.

It grew out of sketches for a showpiece for violin and orchestra on Spanish themes. He decided the tunes would do better in a work for the whole orchestra, and kept a part for solo violin among many other solos. The themes are real Spanish dance tunes; the opening one comes from a published collection of Spanish folk music.

At the first rehearsal, he wrote, the orchestra had hardly finished the first movement when it began to applaud. He asked the players for permission to dedicate the piece to them, and the printed score lists all 67 of them by name. The premiere, in St Petersburg in the autumn of 1887 with the composer conducting, ended with an insistent encore.

People praised the orchestration, and Rimsky-Korsakov thought they missed the point. The Capriccio, he wrote, is “a brilliant composition for the orchestra”: the changes of colour, the solo cadenzas and the rhythm of the percussion are the music itself, “not its garb”.
The five movements are played without a break, in two groups: I–III, then IV–V.
bigPicture.inOneLine: a dawn song (I), a set of variations (II), the dawn song again (III), a gypsy scene with five cadenzas (IV) and a whirling dance from Asturias (V).

movements.heading: Alborada: Vivo e strepitoso
movements.title: Alborada: Vivo e strepitoso
movements.summary: An [[alborada|alborada]] is a morning song, a dance to greet the sunrise, here in the manner of Asturias in northern Spain. This one bursts out at full force, in A major: a stamping, two-beat dance for the whole orchestra with ringing percussion. A clarinet and then a solo violin answer with quick, showy runs, and the violin closes the movement quietly.

mainIdeas.name: The alborada tune
mainIdeas.description: a bright, stamping dance theme in a fast two-beat rhythm.

mainIdeas.name: The solos
mainIdeas.description: quick, decorated runs for the clarinet and the solo violin.

stops.hear: The whole orchestra bursts in with a bright, stamping dance
A clarinet plays fast, curling runs over the dance
The solo violin takes the lead with its own runs

stops.label: Last 10 seconds
stops.hear: The violin trails off quietly

notice: Listen to the percussion from the first bar. Rimsky-Korsakov said the rhythm of the percussion is part of the music itself, not decoration.

movements.heading: Variazioni: Andante con moto
movements.title: Variazioni: Andante con moto
movements.summary: A gentle tune, first in the horns, then passed from section to section in a set of [[variation|variation]]s. Each time it gets a new colour and a new mood: serene, then a little mournful, then rising to a climax, then calm again. The movement ends with a slow, slithering line in the flute.

mainIdeas.name: The theme
mainIdeas.description: a simple, singing Spanish folk melody, first heard in the horns.

stops.hear: The horns sing a warm, simple melody
The strings take over the tune, with new lines around it
The woodwinds come forward, the mood turns a little sad
The whole orchestra builds to a full, warm climax
Quieter again; solo instruments in front

stops.label: Last 30 seconds
stops.hear: A flute winds slowly up and down in small, sliding steps

notice: Follow the melody from instrument to instrument. The tune hardly changes; what changes is who plays it and what surrounds it, which is the point of the whole piece.

movements.heading: Alborada
movements.title: Alborada
movements.summary: The dawn song returns, almost note for note, but in a different key, B-flat major, and with the solos swapped: now the violin goes first and the clarinet answers. Rimsky-Korsakov later admitted that here the brass can drown the woodwinds, and advised conductors to play it a little less loudly.

mainIdeas.description: The alborada tune, as in movement I, in new colours.

stops.hear: The stamping dance again, in the full orchestra
The solo violin’s runs
The clarinet answers

stops.label: Last 10 seconds
stops.hear: A loud, sudden ending
stops.happening: The end of the first part

notice: Compare it with the first movement. The tune is the same; listen to how much the different key and the swapped soloists change its colour.

movements.heading: Scena e canto gitano: Allegretto
movements.title: Scena e canto gitano: Allegretto
movements.summary: A gypsy scene and song. Over drum rolls, five free, unaccompanied [[cadenza|cadenza]]s follow one another: first the horns and trumpets with a fanfare, then the solo violin, the flute, the clarinet and finally the harp, with the triangle. Then the gypsy song begins, a swaying dance in three beats, while the string players pluck chords like guitarists.

mainIdeas.name: The fanfare
mainIdeas.description: a call for horns and trumpets over a drum roll.

mainIdeas.name: The cadenzas
mainIdeas.description: short solo flights for the brass, violin, flute, clarinet and harp.

mainIdeas.name: The gypsy song
mainIdeas.description: a passionate, swaying dance tune in three beats, with the strings imitating guitars.

stops.hear: A drum roll, then a fanfare in the horns and trumpets
stops.happening: The scene opens: the first cadenza

stops.hear: The solo violin plays alone, freely
The flute, then the clarinet, each with a solo flight over a soft drum roll
The harp ripples up and down, with the tinkle of a triangle
A swaying, passionate dance tune over plucked, strummed chords in the strings
stops.happening: The gypsy song; violins and violas marked *quasi guitara*, “like a guitar”

stops.hear: The fanfare returns between verses of the song, and the dance gathers speed

stops.label: Last 30 seconds
stops.hear: Faster and louder, without a break

notice: Listen to the strings during the gypsy song. They are not bowing but plucking chords in [[pizzicato|pizzicato]], to sound like a group of guitars.

movements.heading: Fandango asturiano
movements.title: Fandango asturiano
movements.summary: A [[fandango|fandango]], a fast Spanish dance in three beats, here from Asturias in the north of Spain. The trombones begin the tune and the woodwinds finish it; castanets click throughout. The dance whirls faster and faster, and at the end the alborada of the first movement bursts back in to finish the piece.

mainIdeas.name: The fandango tune
mainIdeas.description: a vigorous, clicking dance in three beats, first half in the trombones, second half in the woodwinds.

mainIdeas.name: The alborada
mainIdeas.description: the opening dance, returning as the finale’s climax.

stops.hear: The trombones start a vigorous dance tune; the woodwinds finish it; castanets click
The tune passes through the orchestra, each time in a new colour
The dance moves through ever-changing colours and grows wilder
The stamping alborada tune from the first movement returns

stops.label: Last 20 seconds
stops.hear: Very fast, to a brilliant final crash

notice: Listen for the moment when the fandango turns into the alborada tune from the start. The piece ends where it began, only louder and faster.

notes.title: In this recording
notes.body: Doráti’s recording for Mercury’s Living Presence series was made with the London Symphony Orchestra in Watford Town Hall in June 1959. On Spotify each of the five movements is its own track, although they follow one another without a break.

threads.title: A concerto for the orchestra
threads.body: Nearly every player has a solo moment: clarinet and violin in the alboradas, horns in the variations, five cadenzas in the gypsy scene, trombones in the fandango.

threads.title: Spain seen from Russia
threads.body: Glinka had travelled in Spain and written overtures on the tunes he collected there; Rimsky-Korsakov follows him, with real folk melodies but a Russian orchestra’s colours.

threads.title: Beginning and end
threads.body: The alborada opens the piece, returns in the middle and comes back to finish it, so that the whole Capriccio swings around one dance.
